newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - Portuguese archaeologists dive on ships' graveyard.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Portuguese archaeologists dive on ships' graveyard.

text.p: Portuguese archaeologists are braving treacherous currents in the murky sea near Lisbon to dive for treasures in a ships' graveyard.
The ocean bed off the 17th century Sao Juliao da Barra fortress is littered with the remains of ships sunk over the ages.
Some were 16th and 17th century Portuguese merchant vessels returning home from India and Africa heavily laden with goods and bruised by storms and attacks by pirates.

Visibility on the sea bed is just 1.5 metres (four feet) and currents are so strong that a team from the state-funded Portuguese Institute of Archaeology and Heritage (IPPAR) had to cling onto ropes on a recent dive to avoid being swept onto the rocks of the fortress.

The sea is polluted with industrial waste and chemicals, unlike the coast farther from Lisbon where visibility was much better. IPPAR's team, who dive every day -- weather permitting -- are inoculated against hepatitis.
SOME 50 WRECKS LIE OFF SAO JULIAO

Francisco Alves, IPPAR's chief archaeologist, said some 50 ships had sunk, mostly victims of underwater sand dunes or storms, in the harsh Atlantic seas off Sao Juliao da Barra, which is located at the mouth of the River Tagus.

"Many ships, filled to the brim with goods, with sails torn and constantly having to pump out water, could hardly navigate by the time they reached the Portuguese coast and ran into sand dunes and rocks," said Alves.
The currents broke up the ships, scattering debris across the ocean bed, which changes every time the divers return.
"When we find bits of wreckage, it is often impossible to identify which ship they came from," Alves said.
Hundreds of people had died in the shipwrecks off Sao Juliao da Barra, 10 miles (six km) from Lisbon, he said.
The most tragic case was the loss of Portuguese merchant vessel "Nossa Senhora dos Martires" in a storm in 1606. Archives say more than 300 people on board died and there were no survivors.
FINDINGS WILL BE SHOWN AT WORLD FAIR
IPPAR plans to display its undersea findings from Sao Juliao da Barra at the Portuguese pavilion at the Lisbon Expo World Fair next year. The theme of the fair is the world's oceans.
The display will include two astrolabes, brass cannons, Chinese porcelain and pottery, pepper and coins.
Astrolabes, graduated circular discs with a sighting device, were used to measure the altitude of stars and planets and as a navigational aid.

"Most of the ships sunk off Sao Juliao da Barra were on their way home after long voyages, rather than setting off from Lisbon," Alves said. "Returning ships are much more interesting for archaeologists as they carried goods from abroad," he added.

The archaeological treasures are cleaned, registered and stored at a warehouse at Belem, a suburb of Lisbon along the banks of the Tagus and the departure point for many of the early Portuguese explorers.
Gnarled brass cannons, jugs and worn planks from a 15th century 30-metre (100-feet) cargo vessel, found under the Lisbon metro system near the Tagus, cover the warehouse floor.
IPPAR has exclusive rights to search for archaeological treasures off Sao Juliao da Barra and freelance "treasure hunters" are banned from diving there, Alves said.

"We won't have treasure hunters stripping our ships," said IPPAR manager Luis Felipe Castro. "Our archaeological heritage must be protected. Archaeologists must be able to study our findings. The sailing ships in the 16th and 17th centuries were the most advanced form of machinery of their time."
IPPAR's other projects include a study of the remains of 14th and 15th century cargo vessels found in Lisbon and near the city of Aveiro in central Portugal.
